text: NIST's current password guidance, SP 800-63B, overturned decades of password-policy folk wisdom: it favors length over complexity, requires screening every password against known-breached lists, and drops forced periodic rotation unless there's real evidence of compromise.

A modern, NIST-aligned policy sets a minimum length of 12 or more characters and encourages passphrases, which are both easier to remember and harder to crack than a short, mangled string. It drops the mandatory mix of uppercase, digits, and symbols entirely. It screens every new password against breached-password lists at creation time — using a service like Have I Been Pwned's Pwned Passwords API or a built-in identity-provider feature — and rejects any match outright. And it doesn't force a reset on a fixed calendar; it waits for specific evidence that an account's password has actually been exposed.

Side by side, the shift is stark. The old policy demanded only 8 characters, a mixed-case-digit-symbol combination, and a reset every 90 days regardless of actual risk. The new policy asks for longer passwords, drops the composition mandate entirely, screens against real breach data at the point of creation, and only forces rotation when a compromise is confirmed — not on a timer that resets for everyone whether or not anything happened.

Complexity rules backfired because they collided with human memory instead of working with it. Forced to include a digit and a symbol, people didn't invent stronger secrets — they transformed the same base word in predictable, well-documented ways: Password becomes Password1, then Password1!, and at the next forced rotation, P@ssw0rd1!. Password-cracking tools know this exact substitution chain cold, so the added complexity bought very little real security while making the password noticeably harder for a human to remember and type correctly.
